- If sentiment history shows a recent negative signal (e.g., -1.00), model should reduce forecast slope or avoid upward bias.
- When model forecasts are rising steadily (e.g., +0.01–0.03 per day) but true prices drop sharply, cap forecast growth after 3–5 days of upward trend.
- If true prices show a sharp downward spike (e.g., >5% drop from prior peak), model should not overcorrect or overshoot downward — avoid predicting below 50% of prior high.
- If sentiment is neutral or positive (0.00–0.20), model should not assume mean reversion — allow for continued drift unless confirmed by price action.
- If model forecasts are flat or slightly rising but true prices fall >10% from 30-day average, adjust downward by 1–2% per day until price stabilizes.
- Avoid forecasting above 65% of prior 30-day high unless sentiment confirms strong bullish momentum.
- If true price drops below 50% of prior 30-day high, model should not forecast above 50% of that low — avoid “rebound overcorrection.”
- If sentiment history includes multiple -1.00 entries, model should not forecast upward trend — expect continued decline or consolidation.
- If model forecasts are rising but true prices show a “V-shaped” recovery, reduce forecast slope by 50% until price stabilizes above 50% of prior low.
- If sentiment is positive (0.20+) and model forecasts are flat, increase forecast by 0.01–0.02 per day to reflect bullish sentiment.
